plain_english: You need to be careful when choosing who to spend time with. Ask yourself: are these people worth giving part of your life to? Or will you just waste your time and theirs? Some people actually think you owe them something when you try to help them. Athenodorus said he wouldn't even eat dinner with someone who wasn't grateful for the invitation. He meant that he certainly wouldn't dine with people who think a fancy meal repays their friends' kindness. These hosts treat expensive dishes like generous gifts, as if stuffing themselves honors their guests. Take away their audience, and they won't enjoy eating alone at all.
original_excerpt: In all cases one should be careful in one's choice of men, and see whether they be worthy of our bestowing a part of our life upon them, or whether we shall waste our own time and theirs also: for some even consider us to be in their debt because of our services to them. Athenodorus said that "he would not so much as dine with a man who would not be grateful to him for doing so": meaning, I imagine, that much less would he go to dinner with those who recompense the services of their friends by their table, and regard courses of dishes as donatives, as if they overate themselves to do honour to others. Take away from these men their witnesses and spectators: they will take no pleasure in solitary gluttony.

plain_english: You need to figure out what suits you better: taking bold action or quiet thinking and reflection. Then go with whatever your natural talents pull you toward. Isocrates once grabbed his student Ephorus and dragged him away from the public forum. He thought the young man would do better work writing histories. There's no point in forcing your mind to do work that doesn't fit you. Fighting against your nature is useless.
original_excerpt: You must decide whether your disposition is better suited for vigorous action or for tranquil speculation and contemplation, and you must adopt whichever the bent of your genius inclines you for. Isocrates laid hands upon Ephorus and led him away from the forum, thinking that he would be more usefully employed in compiling chronicles; for no good is done by forcing one's mind to engage in uncongenial work: it is vain to struggle against Nature.

plain_english: Nothing brings more joy to the mind than a true and pleasant friendship. What a blessing it is to have someone you can trust with all your secrets. Someone whose opinion of you matters less than your own conscience. Someone whose conversation eases your worries, whose advice helps your plans, whose good spirits lift your mood, and whose very presence makes you happy!
original_excerpt: Yet nothing delights the mind so much as faithful and pleasant friendship: what a blessing it is when there is one whose breast is ready to receive all your secrets with safety, whose knowledge of your actions you fear less than your own conscience, whose conversation removes your anxieties, whose advice assists your plans, whose cheerfulness dispels your gloom, whose very sight delights you!

plain_english: We should choose friends who are free from strong desires as much as possible. Vices spread like diseases. They pass from one person to their neighbor and harm anyone who gets close. During a plague, we're careful not to sit near infected people whose disease is raging. We know we'll be in danger and might catch the plague from their breath. The same goes for choosing friends. We must pick people who are as clean from corruption as possible. The surest way to create disease is to mix what is healthy with what is rotten.
original_excerpt: We should choose for our friends men who are, as far as possible, free from strong desires: for vices are contagious, and pass from a man to his neighbour, and injure those who touch them. As, therefore, in times of pestilence we have to be careful not to sit near people who are infected and in whom the disease is raging, because by so doing, we shall run into danger and catch the plague from their very breath; so, too, in choosing our friends' dispositions, we must take care to select those who are as far as may be unspotted by the world; for the way to breed disease is to mix what is sound with what is rotten.

plain_english: But I don't advise you to seek out only wise men as companions. Where would you find one? We've been looking for centuries without success. Instead of the perfect person, choose the one who is least flawed. You'd be hard-pressed to find a better time for choosing good people than if you could pick from among Plato, Xenophon, and the other students of Socrates. Or if you could choose from Cato's era — a time that produced many men worthy of living alongside Cato. That age also produced some of the worst villains history has ever known, planners of terrible crimes. It needed both types to make Cato's greatness clear. It needed good men for him to win over, and bad men for him to prove his strength against. But today, when good people are so rare, you can't afford to be picky.
original_excerpt: Yet I do not advise you to follow after or draw to yourself no one except a wise man: for where will you find him whom for so many centuries we have sought in vain? in the place of the best possible man take him who is least bad. You would hardly find any time that would have enabled you to make a happier choice than if you could have sought for a good man from among the Platos and Xenophons and the rest of the produce of the brood of Socrates, or if you had been permitted to choose one from the age of Cato: an age which bore many men worthy to be born in Cato's time (just as it also bore many men worse than were ever known before, planners of the blackest crimes: for it needed both classes in order to make Cato understood: it wanted both good men, that he might win their approbation, and bad men, against whom he could prove his strength): but at the present day, when there is such a dearth of good men, you must be less squeamish in your choice.

plain_english: Above all, stay away from gloomy people who complain about everything that happens. They find fault with whatever comes their way. Even if they remain loyal friends to you, a bitter companion will destroy your peace of mind. They greet every situation with a groan.
original_excerpt: Above all, however, avoid dismal men who grumble at whatever happens, and find something to complain of in everything. Though he may continue loyal and friendly towards you, still one's peace of mind is destroyed by a comrade whose mind is soured and who meets every incident with a groan.
